text: Building Vietnam's next growth engine
Vietnam is increasingly viewed as an important manufacturing and export base in Asia.
What is changing in the country's role in global supply chains, and how durable is that position?
Vietnam has moved beyond being seen simply as a competitive production location.

It is increasingly becoming an important node in regional supply chains, supported by its manufacturing capacity, expanding consumer market, network of trade agreements, and proximity to major Asian economies.
Multinational companies are reassessing production, sourcing, and distribution networks across Asia.
They're looking for a balance between efficiency, resilience, and access to customers.
Vietnam is well placed in sectors such as electronics, consumer goods, textiles, machinery, food processing, and export-oriented services.

Its participation in agreements such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), the EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) also supports market access and strengthens its role in regional trade.
The scale of this opportunity is reflected in Vietnam's trade and investment performance.

In the first ten months of this year, its total export and import turnover reached $1.01 trillion, surpassing the $1 trillion milestone for the first time, while registered FDI reached nearly $55 billion; the highest level in 17 years.
The country's foreign-invested sector remains an important contributor to exports, while the next challenge is to ensure that more domestic businesses participate in these value chains.
The position is durable, but not automatic.
Vietnam must continue investing in infrastructure, energy reliability, logistics, digital connectivity, and workforce skills.
Labor costs will naturally rise as the economy develops, so competitiveness must increasingly come from productivity, quality, technology, and speed, not cost alone.
The next step is to deepen the domestic ecosystem around foreign-invested enterprises.
Vietnamese businesses need support to meet international standards on quality, scale, compliance, traceability, and sustainability.
That is how the country can move from assembly toward design, engineering, R&D, advanced manufacturing, and higher-value services.
Vietnam's next phase of growth will also require substantial funding.

To sustain double-digit growth between 2026 and 2030, the Ministry of Finance (MoF) estimates that total social investment will need to reach around VND38,500 trillion ($1.5 billion), or more than double the level recorded during 2021-2025.
Diversifying funding sources across bank finance, capital markets, foreign investment, development finance, and other channels will be important.
Vietnam is strengthening its role in global manufacturing and supply chains.
What will determine whether it can move further up the value chain?
Vietnam's progress has been remarkable.
The economy grew by almost 10 per cent year-on-year in the third quarter, one of the fastest rates in Asia.
Manufacturing continues to expand at double-digit rates, and electronics shipments have surged on the back of the AI-driven technology cycle.
Moving further up the value chain is the next challenge, and it depends on a few connected factors.
The first is the depth of the local supplier ecosystem.
The more domestic companies can supply components, services, and engineering to multinational manufacturers, the more value stays in Vietnam and the more resilient supply chains become.
The second is people.
Skills, technology adoption, research capability, and management expertise allow a country to progress from assembly toward design, engineering, and higher-value production.
The third is infrastructure.
Logistics, ports, power, and digital connectivity all need to keep pace with industrial growth.
Vietnam's priorities are clear: lift productivity, build workforce capability, and attract higher-value production.
The country has the momentum.
Sustaining it will depend on investing in the capabilities that make the next stage possible.
Vietnamese companies are increasingly looking beyond the domestic market.
Which capabilities will determine whether domestic champions can expand successfully across Asia and beyond?

According to HSBC's latest Trade Pulse survey, Vietnamese businesses are among the most confident surveyed about the outlook for international trade, with 94 per cent expecting their international trade to grow over the next two years.
Successful international expansion starts with a clear market entry strategy.
Companies need to understand where their customers are, how regulations work, which partners they need, how supply chains operate, and how profits can be repatriated.
Entering a market because it appears attractive is not enough; the business model must be viable locally.
The scale of the opportunity is considerable.
Vietnam's total outward FDI reached $3.41 billion, more than tripling year-on-year, with growth of 3.1-fold.
But expansion needs to be supported by the right operating infrastructure from the outset.
Risk management is equally important.
Companies need to assess foreign exchange, political, legal, tax, sanctions, cybersecurity, and repatriation risks before expansion accelerates.
Treasury, payments, and cash management capabilities should be established early, rather than treated as an afterthought once the business is already operating across borders.
Talent is another differentiator.
Vietnamese companies need local knowledge in each market while maintaining consistent group-wide governance, financial controls, and risk standards.
The most effective model often combines local decision-making with clear central oversight.
Partnerships can shorten the learning curve.
Local distributors, suppliers, advisers, technology providers, and financial institutions can help companies understand market practices and avoid preventable mistakes.
Regional networks also allow businesses to test demand and build capability progressively.
International banks like HSBC can support the journey from initial market assessment through to sustained operations.
For example, we have accompanied FPT on its international expansion journey since 2005, supporting the company with working capital, international trade, and cross-border payments, among other areas.
However, the role of an international bank extends beyond the provision of financial services.
More importantly, it is about connecting clients with international opportunities, underpinned by local insight, disciplined risk management, and a long-term commitment.

With operations in 56 markets and a presence in markets and regions that conducted 86 per cent of world trade in 2025, HSBC can connect Vietnamese companies to local expertise, payment infrastructure, foreign exchange solutions, trade finance, working capital facilities, and financing for acquisitions or overseas operations.
The key message is that internationalization is not a single transaction.
It is an operating capability that must be built and strengthened over time.
Looking ahead, what should Vietnam's business leaders do over the next three to five years to capture global opportunities while managing greater uncertainty?
Vietnamese business leaders should treat resilience, liquidity, and risk management as strategic capabilities.
These are no longer issues that can sit solely within finance or operations.
They influence growth, customer confidence and the ability to respond when conditions change.
First, companies should invest in skills, technology, data quality, and governance.
Strong data enables better forecasting and faster decisions.
Good governance builds trust with customers, investors, lenders, and international partners.
Skills development will determine whether Vietnam captures higher-value opportunities rather than remaining focused on lower-value activities.
Second, businesses should build relationships across regional trade corridors and diversify customers and suppliers where appropriate.
This does not mean abandoning successful markets.
It means reducing excessive concentration and creating options.
Third, companies should prepare for higher expectations around sustainability, traceability, product standards, emissions, labor practices, and compliance.
These requirements are increasingly linked to market access and customer relationships, not simply corporate reporting.
Fourth, funding structures should match the duration and risk of each investment.
Short-term working capital needs, long-term infrastructure, acquisitions, technology investment, and overseas expansion should not all be financed in the same way.
A diversified funding strategy can improve resilience and support responsible growth.
Finally, policymakers, financial institutions, and corporates need to work together.
Policymakers can strengthen infrastructure, skills, regulation, and market access.
Financial institutions can provide capital, risk management tools, and international connectivity.
Corporates must invest in productivity, governance, and people.

According to figures from the MoF, Vietnam's labor productivity in 2025 was estimated at around 60 per cent of Thailand's level, 40 per cent of Malaysia's, and less than 10 per cent of Singapore's. These numbers highlight substantial room for improvement.
